title: The Day Whitey Basson Told Shoprite's Shareholders He Was Tired
dek: Thirty-seven years after buying eight Cape grocery stores, Whitey Basson stepped down from Shoprite and gave the plainest reason there is.

story.event: Announcing his retirement as chief executive at the 2016 annual meeting, saying he was tired
story.summary: At Shoprite's annual meeting on 31 October 2016, Whitey Basson, who had built the grocer from eight Cape stores bought in 1979-80 for about R1 million, announced he would retire as chief executive at the end of the year, saying he was tired. Analysts linked his exit to chairman Christo Wiese's wish to merge Shoprite with Steinhoff, which Basson had questioned; both men denied it, and the merger talks were later abandoned.
paragraphs: On Monday 31 October 2016, at Shoprite's annual meeting in Parow, Cape Town, Whitey Basson told investors he would retire as chief executive at the end of the year. He was 70. In late 1979, as an executive of Pep Stores, he had begun negotiating to buy an eight-store Cape grocer from the Rogut family, whose members had fallen out; the business cost about R1 million. By 2016 Shoprite had more than 2,200 stores, about 140,000 workers and a market value of R115 billion.

He gave reporters a plain reason: "I am tired", he said, because "the business is now so large and there are so many issues that take up too much time." To the Financial Mail he said he was fighting on several fronts, and added: "You need to be young." His chief operating officer, Pieter Engelbrecht, 47, who had once been his personal assistant, would take over on 1 January; Basson said Engelbrecht already handled about half of the operating issues. Basson would stay on as non-executive vice-chairman.

Not everyone took the reason at face value. Christo Wiese, Shoprite's chairman and largest shareholder, also held the largest stake in the furniture group Steinhoff, and had called a merger of the two a "natural development". Basson had made his doubts public: "What would you benefit by putting Anglo American and Toyota together?" Analysts read his departure as clearing the way; both men said the deal was not the reason. The same meeting heard criticism of his pay, R100 million that year including a R50 million bonus, and almost 30 per cent of votes went against the pay policy.

Talks to fold Steinhoff's African businesses into Shoprite were abandoned in 2017 when the two sides could not agree a price. Asked whether he was pleased, Basson replied: "Are you asking if the Pope is Catholic?" Shoprite bought back his shares, about 1.5 per cent of the company, for R1.75 billion. Steinhoff then set out to take voting control of Shoprite through a new listed subsidiary, until, late that year, the accounting problems its auditors had questioned set off the collapse of Steinhoff's share price.

quote.text: our duty is not to lay action aside, like a lyre of too high a pitch, but to lower the key and adapt it to such forms of public effort as are light, unexacting, and within an old man's compass.
quote.work: Moralia: On Old Men in Public Life (An seni respublica gerenda sit)
quote.source_title: Selected Essays of Plutarch, Vol. I, tr. T. G. Tucker, Project Gutenberg eBook #62618
quote.connection: Plutarch argues that age should lower the pitch of public work, not end it, and Basson, staying on as vice-chairman, half followed him. But his other remark, that the job needed someone young, pulls the other way, and the story does not say which instinct was wiser.

reflection: Basson gave the simplest reason there is, and many people did not believe him. Perhaps the merger mattered too; the record does not settle it. But a man who had worked flat out for decades saying that he was tired is not a riddle that needs solving.

You are near the start of your road, not the end. Even so, tiredness is information, not a confession. When you notice it, it is worth saying so plainly to someone who shares the work, before it turns into a decision that gets made for you.
invitation: Tell one person who shares your work, at the office or at home, how tired you actually are this week, in one honest sentence, and ask which single task could come off your plate.

cross_checks.claim: Basson announced at Shoprite's annual meeting on 31 October 2016 that he would retire at the end of the year, saying he was tired.
Shoprite began as an eight-store Cape grocer bought from the Rogut family for about R1 million at the end of the 1970s.
Basson publicly doubted a Shoprite-Steinhoff merger ('Anglo American and Toyota').
Basson's pay that year was about R100 million including a R50 million bonus.

research_notes: Episode changed from the slate. The slate named the 1979 purchase of eight Cape Town stores. That deal is documented only in outline: no accessible source records Basson's own account of the decision or what he knew at the time, Shoprite's own profile of him refuses automated requests, and the reviews of Niel Joubert's biography give only the bare facts. His 2016 retirement is documented in his own words by Bloomberg and the Financial Mail and in detail by TJ Strydom's biography of Wiese, so the edition tells that, with the 1979 purchase as background. Dates of the purchase differ: Crotty says negotiations began in late 1979 and that he 'in 1980 took eight stores'; other reports give May or November 1979; Bloomberg says he formed the company in 1979. The story says negotiations began in late 1979 and gives no completion date. Price: about R1 million in Crotty and in Wiese's own words. Size in 2016: Bloomberg gives a market value of R115 billion and more than 140,000 workers; Crotty gives a value of R152 billion and 137,775 staff; the story uses Bloomberg's figures and Crotty's 'more than 2,200 stores'. Stake: Crotty says 1.6% worth R1.77 billion at the time of the announcement; Strydom says about 1.5%, bought back for R1.75 billion; the story uses Strydom's figures for the buy-back. Age: Crotty says 70, Bloomberg that he turned 71 in January; both fit. After the announcement: Bloomberg says he would stay as non-executive vice-chairman, Crotty that he would be on call for consulting under his notice period. Reasons: Basson gave weariness; Crotty reports analysts' view that the Steinhoff plan was the real reason; Strydom says both he and Wiese denied the deal was the reason. The story gives all three without choosing. Steinhoff: the story says only that the accounting problems its auditors had questioned set off the collapse of its share price late in 2017, as Strydom describes, and attributes no wrongdoing to any person. Crotty's piece also reports criticism of Shoprite's employment conditions, which the story does not cover. The Plutarch passage advises an elderly statesman, not a businessman; it is applied by analogy.
